hints: Remember what an ideal gas pretends, that particles have no volume and no attractions at all, so focus on which gas breaks those rules most.
Compare polarity and size, $\text{HCl}$ is polar with permanent dipole-dipole forces while $\text{He}$, $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{N}_2$ are all non-polar with only weak London forces.
The gas with the strongest intermolecular forces and largest effective attractions will stick together most and deviate most, so pick the polar molecule.
walkthrough:
**Recall what ideal means**

An ideal gas assumes two things. Particles have zero volume, and there are zero forces between them.

Real gases deviate when particles are larger or attract each other:
$$\text{greater intermolecular forces} \rightarrow \text{greater deviation}$$

**Compare the four gases**

Look at polarity, which controls strength of attractions. $\text{He}$ is tiny and non-polar, $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{N}_2$ are small non-polar molecules with only weak London dispersion forces.

$\text{HCl}$ is different, it is polar with a permanent dipole, $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$, so it has extra dipole-dipole attractions plus London forces.

**Pick the biggest deviator**

Stronger attractions mean molecules pull together, occupy effective volume, and are easiest to liquefy. That is furthest from ideal.

$\text{HCl}$ has the strongest intermolecular forces and the highest boiling point of the four, so it deviates most.

options.A: Correct. $\text{HCl}$ is polar and has permanent dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces. These significant attractions violate the ideal assumption of no intermolecular forces, so it deviates most.
options.B: Not correct. $\text{He}$ is a tiny, non-polar single atom with only extremely weak London forces and a very low boiling point. It is closest to ideal, not furthest, so students choosing this confuse smallest with most deviating.
options.C: Not correct. $\text{CH}_4$ is non-polar with only weak London dispersion forces. It deviates a little more than $\text{He}$ because it is larger, but much less than polar $\text{HCl}$.
options.D: Not correct. $\text{N}_2$ is non-polar with only London forces. Although it is heavier than $\text{CH}_4$ and $\text{He}$, it has no dipole and much weaker attractions than $\text{HCl}$, so its deviation is small.
